role: Commander at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah and other campaigns
summary: Amr ibn al-As (RA) was one of the most brilliant military commanders and diplomats among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. He accepted Islam in the year 8 AH after a long period of opposition, rapidly rose to military command, and led the Muslim conquest of Egypt — a campaign he conducted with minimal force and remarkable speed, opening one of the most strategically significant territories in the early Islamic state.
biography:
Amr ibn al-As ibn Wa'il al-Qurashi al-Sahmi was born in Makkah around 573 CE into the Banu Sahm clan of Quraysh. He came from a family of traders and diplomats, and from a young age he demonstrated exceptional political intelligence and oratory. Before Islam, he was among the Quraysh's most capable envoys, famously dispatched to the Negus of Abyssinia to demand the return of the early Muslim emigrants. His mission failed — the Negus was moved by Ja'far ibn Abi Talib's recitation of the Quran and refused to return the Muslims. This encounter left a deep impression on Amr.

Amr was a persistent opponent of the Prophet ﷺ for many years and participated in the Quraysh's hostilities against the early Muslim community. However, his intellectual honesty and strategic mind eventually led him to recognize the truth of Islam. According to al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', Amr journeyed to accept Islam in 8 AH (630 CE), shortly before the Conquest of Makkah, traveling alongside Khalid ibn al-Walid and Uthman ibn Talha — both also new converts at that time. When Amr presented himself to the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet stretched out his hand and Amr said: 'I want to give you my pledge on condition that my past sins are forgiven.' The Prophet ﷺ replied: 'Do you not know that Islam erases what came before it, and hijrah erases what came before it?' (Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Iman)

Despite his late conversion, the Prophet ﷺ immediately recognized Amr's extraordinary abilities and gave him significant responsibility. He was appointed commander of the expedition to Dhat al-Salasil (8 AH), a sensitive military mission to the Syrian frontier. Notably, the Prophet ﷺ later added Abu Bakr and Umar to the expedition's forces — yet kept Amr as commander rather than replacing him with these senior Companions, a decision that demonstrated the Prophet's confidence in Amr's leadership.

Abu Bakr and Umar ibn al-Khattab continued to rely heavily on Amr as a military commander during the early conquests. His most celebrated achievement was the conquest of Egypt. In 18 AH (639 CE), Amr ibn al-As requested permission from Umar to march against Byzantine Egypt, arguing it was strategically vulnerable. After initial hesitation, Umar granted permission. Amr led a relatively small force — historical sources suggest approximately 4,000 fighters — across the Sinai. He took Pelusium (al-Farama), then the Roman fortress of Babylon (near modern Cairo) after a siege, and finally Alexandria, the second city of the Byzantine Empire. The conquest was completed by around 20 AH (641 CE). Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah notes that Amr's conquest of Egypt stands as one of the most rapid and geopolitically consequential expansions in the early Islamic state.

Amr ibn al-As served as the first governor of Egypt, establishing the garrison city of Fustat (forerunner of modern Cairo) as the administrative capital. Under his governance, Egypt became a stable and prosperous province. He reopened the ancient canal connecting the Nile to the Red Sea — a project that had fallen into disuse under the Byzantines — facilitating grain shipments to the Hijaz, particularly during times of drought. Umar ibn al-Khattab praised this achievement.

Amr was later involved in the political conflicts of the fitnah period. He aligned with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan during the dispute with Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) and served as an adviser and envoy during this turbulent period. Classical Sunni scholarship, including al-Dhahabi and Ibn Kathir, records this period with acknowledgment of its complexity and does not render judgment on the sincere companions who differed in their political positions.

Amr ibn al-As died in Fustat (Egypt) in 43 AH (664 CE). A moving account preserved in Sahih Muslim records his deathbed reflection: 'When I was a mushrik (non-Muslim), no one was more hostile to the Prophet ﷺ than I was. If I had died in that state I would have been in the Fire. When Allah gave me the love of Islam, I came to the Prophet ﷺ... I wish I had been tested more as a Muslim.' His repentance was sincere and his service to Islam was immense.
